title: HTTP/2 & HTTP/3: A Study-Notes Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to modern HTTP transport: how HTTP/1.1's limits forced binary framing and multiplexing, how HPACK and QPACK compress headers, how QUIC over UDP kills transport-level head-of-line blocking, and when each version actually helps.

chapters.title: Why HTTP/1.1 Ran Out of Road
points: HTTP is a request/response protocol; versions differ in *wire encoding and transport*, not in semantics (methods, status codes, headers are unchanged across 1.1/2/3 — RFC 9110 defines shared semantics)
HTTP/1.1 is a plaintext, line-oriented protocol: request line + CRLF-separated headers + blank line + body
One TCP connection carries one in-flight request at a time; the response must complete before the next begins
Application-level head-of-line blocking: a slow 2 MB image response stalls every queued request behind it on that connection
Pipelining (sending request 2 before response 1 arrives) was specified but responses must return in order, so it never removed HOL blocking; broken proxies made it unusable and browsers disabled it
Browser workaround: 6 parallel TCP connections per origin — 6× handshakes, 6× congestion-control slow starts, 6× server sockets
Each new TCP connection starts with a small congestion window (~10 packets, ~14 KB), so parallel connections compete instead of sharing bandwidth intelligently
Sharding workaround: serve assets from img1.example.com, img2.example.com to unlock more parallel connections; multiplies DNS lookups and TLS handshakes
Concatenation workaround: bundle all JS into one file, sprite all icons into one image — one big request beats many small ones, but breaks caching granularity
Inlining workaround: base64 data: URIs embed images in CSS; ~33% size penalty and the asset can never be cached separately
Header overhead: every request repeats Cookie, User-Agent, Accept, Referer as plaintext — often 500–1500 bytes per request, uncompressed, while a request body may be 0 bytes
For a page with 100 sub-resources, repeated headers can exceed the size of the HTML itself
Cost model: latency (RTT), not bandwidth, dominates page load — doubling bandwidth barely helps, halving RTT nearly halves load time
SPDY (Google, 2009) prototyped multiplexing + header compression over TLS and became the basis of HTTP/2 (RFC 7540, 2015; revised as RFC 9113)
Mental model to carry through the handbook: HTTP/1.1 fixed the *format*; HTTP/2 fixed the *connection*; HTTP/3 fixed the *transport*

chapters.title: HTTP/2 Binary Framing Layer
points: HTTP/2 replaces text with a binary framing layer: the smallest unit is a frame, not a line of ASCII
Frame header is exactly 9 bytes: 24-bit Length, 8-bit Type, 8-bit Flags, 1 reserved bit + 31-bit Stream Identifier
Default max frame payload is 16,384 bytes (2^14), negotiable up to 2^24-1 via SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE
Binary framing means no ambiguous whitespace parsing, no chunked-encoding text scanning — parsers are simpler and immune to request-smuggling tricks that exploit text-length ambiguity
Key frame types: DATA (body bytes), HEADERS (compressed header block), SETTINGS, PRIORITY, RST_STREAM, PUSH_PROMISE, PING, GOAWAY, WINDOW_UPDATE, CONTINUATION
Message = a full request or response, made of one HEADERS frame plus zero or more DATA frames; Stream = a bidirectional numbered flow of frames; Connection = one TCP connection carrying all streams
Hierarchy to memorize: Connection > Streams > Messages > Frames
Client-initiated streams use odd IDs, server-initiated (push) use even; IDs strictly increase and are never reused on a connection
Stream ID 0 is the connection control stream — SETTINGS, PING, GOAWAY, and connection-level WINDOW_UPDATE ride there
Stream lifecycle states: idle → open → half-closed (local/remote) → closed; END_STREAM flag transitions a peer to half-closed

Connection preface: client sends the magic string `PRI * HTTP/2.0

SM

` followed by a SETTINGS frame, so an HTTP/1.1 server chokes early rather than misparsing

SETTINGS is a negotiation of defaults, not a handshake: each side announces its own limits (HEADER_TABLE_SIZE, MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, MAX_FRAME_SIZE, MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE) and must be ACKed
RST_STREAM cancels one stream with an error code without touching the connection — HTTP/1.1 could only close the whole socket
GOAWAY announces graceful shutdown and names the last stream ID the sender will process, so clients know exactly what to retry
Version negotiation: ALPN in the TLS handshake advertises `h2`; the older upgrade dance (`Upgrade: h2c` for cleartext) is effectively unused — every browser requires TLS for HTTP/2

chapters.title: Multiplexing: Many Streams, One Connection
points: Multiplexing = frames from many streams interleave on one connection, each tagged with its stream ID, and are reassembled by ID at the receiver
Requests no longer queue: 100 requests can be in flight at once on a single TCP connection
This removes *application-level* HOL blocking — a slow response no longer blocks other responses, because their frames interleave
Responses may arrive fully out of order relative to request order; there is no positional coupling as in pipelining
One connection per origin means one TCP handshake, one TLS handshake, one congestion window that grows and stays warm
Fewer connections = less server memory and fewer file descriptors, a large win for high-concurrency servers
SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS caps in-flight streams (commonly 100–128); the client queues beyond that, so the cap is the real parallelism limit
Connection coalescing: a client may reuse one h2 connection for multiple hostnames if they resolve to the same IP and the certificate covers both (SAN match)
Consequence: domain sharding becomes an anti-pattern — it splits the connection you wanted to share and defeats coalescing and compression
Concatenation and spriting also become counterproductive: many small cacheable files now cost little, and one changed byte no longer invalidates a giant bundle
Inlining as base64 becomes counterproductive: cost of an extra request has collapsed, but the 33% encoding penalty and lost cacheability remain
Practical migration rule: turning on HTTP/2 while keeping HTTP/1.1 workarounds often yields *no* speedup — remove the workarounds too
Trade-off exposed: putting everything on one TCP connection makes that connection a single point of failure for packet loss (developed in the head-of-line-blocking chapter)
Example wire trace: stream 1 HEADERS, stream 3 HEADERS, stream 1 DATA, stream 5 HEADERS, stream 3 DATA, stream 1 DATA+END_STREAM — three responses progressing simultaneously

chapters.title: Head-of-Line Blocking: Three Layers
points: HOL blocking = the first item in a queue blocks everything behind it, even when the rest could be processed
Layer 1 — HTTP/1.1 application HOL: one response at a time per connection; fixed by HTTP/2 multiplexing
Layer 2 — TCP transport HOL: TCP guarantees a single ordered byte stream, so one lost segment stalls delivery of *all* later bytes to the application, even bytes belonging to other HTTP/2 streams
Why HTTP/2 cannot fix layer 2: the kernel TCP stack has no idea where stream boundaries are; it sees one opaque byte sequence

Concrete case: 10 images multiplexed on one h2 connection, one packet lost — all 10 stall for one RTT of retransmission, whereas 6 separate HTTP/1.1 connections would stall only the one carrying the lost packet
Result: on lossy networks (poor Wi-Fi, congested mobile), HTTP/2 can be *slower* than HTTP/1.1 — measured in real deployments, not just in theory

Layer 3 — TLS record HOL: a TLS record cannot be decrypted until fully received; a record spanning multiple packets stalls on any of them (mitigated by keeping records ≤1 packet, e.g. nginx `ssl_buffer_size 4k`)
QUIC's fix: independent stream reassembly — each stream has its own receive buffer and sequence space, so loss on stream 3 delays only stream 3
QUIC's fix requires leaving TCP behind, which is why HTTP/3 rides UDP (next chapters)
Loss is not uniform: bursty loss hurting many streams' packets weakens QUIC's advantage; isolated loss is where QUIC shines most
HOL blocking also lurks in header compression: HPACK's shared dynamic table forces ordered header processing (see QPACK chapter)
Server-side HOL: a single-threaded handler processing multiplexed streams sequentially reintroduces blocking at the application layer — concurrency must exist above the protocol too
Proxy/CDN HOL: an intermediary terminating h2 and re-fetching over HTTP/1.1 to origin reintroduces layer-1 blocking on the back half
Diagnostic heuristic: if performance drops as loss rate rises but is fine on clean links, suspect transport HOL blocking
Summary table to memorize — HTTP/1.1: app HOL yes, transport HOL yes. HTTP/2: app HOL no, transport HOL yes. HTTP/3: app HOL no, transport HOL no

chapters.title: HPACK: Header Compression in HTTP/2
points: Problem: headers are highly repetitive across requests on the same connection, and gzip-style compression of headers leaks secrets (CRIME attack)
HPACK (RFC 7541) is a purpose-built header compressor: static table + dynamic table + Huffman coding, with no LZ77-style back-references over attacker-mixable data
Static table: 61 predefined entries of common header name/value pairs, identical on every connection — `:method GET` is index 2, `:path /` is index 4
Dynamic table: a per-connection FIFO of previously seen header fields; entries are addressed by index and evicted oldest-first when the size limit is hit
Table size accounting: entry size = name length + value length + 32 bytes of overhead; limit set by SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE, default 4096 bytes
Indexed Header Field representation: one byte can encode an entire `cookie: <long value>` if it is already in the dynamic table

Literal representations come in three flavors: with incremental indexing (adds to table), without indexing (does not), and never-indexed (must not be indexed by any intermediary — for Authorization or session cookies)
Huffman coding: a fixed canonical Huffman table tuned for HTTP header characters compresses literal strings ~30% further; the H bit in the string-length prefix marks it
Integer encoding uses a prefix + continuation scheme so small indexes fit in the leftover bits of the same byte
Pseudo-headers replace the request line and status line: `:method`, `:scheme`, `:authority`, `:path` for requests, `:status` for responses; they must precede regular headers
Header names must be lowercase in HTTP/2 — uppercase is a protocol error (`Content-Type` becomes `content-type`)
`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Upgrade`, `Proxy-Connection` are forbidden; `TE` may only carry `trailers`; connection management is now the framing layer's job

Cookies get special handling: a request's multiple cookie-pairs may be split into separate `cookie` header fields so that individually stable ones stay indexed while a changing one does not evict everything
Measured effect: repeated requests on a warm connection often shrink from ~1400 bytes of headers to under 50, and header traffic can drop 80–90% overall
Security note: HPACK's design deliberately avoids compressing secrets against attacker-controlled text; never-indexed literals are the escape hatch
Gotcha: HPACK state is per-connection and ordered — a proxy must fully decode and re-encode headers, it cannot blindly forward header blocks

chapters.title: Server Push, Priority, and Flow Control
points: Server push: server sends PUSH_PROMISE (reserving an even stream ID) then the response, before the client asks — intended for pushing CSS/JS alongside HTML
Push failed in practice: servers cannot know the client's cache, so pushes are frequently wasted bytes competing with the HTML for bandwidth
Chrome removed HTTP/2 push support in 2022; HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) omits push in practice and the ecosystem moved on
Replacement: `103 Early Hints` with `Link: </style.css>; rel=preload` — server hints the resource, client decides whether it needs it, cache is respected
HTTP/2 priority (RFC 7540): a dependency tree with parent stream IDs, weights 1–256, and exclusive-dependency reparenting
Priority was overcomplicated and inconsistently implemented; servers commonly ignored it, and RFC 9113 deprecated the scheme
Replacement: Extensible Prioritization (RFC 9218) — a simple `priority` header / PRIORITY_UPDATE frame with urgency `u=0..7` and incremental flag `i`
Why priority matters at all: on one shared connection, render-blocking CSS must beat below-the-fold images, otherwise multiplexing can *hurt* first paint by delivering everything equally slowly
Bandwidth-sharing intuition: HTTP/1.1 delivered resources sequentially (each finishes fast); naive round-robin multiplexing finishes everything at once, at the end — the worst outcome for rendering
Flow control is per-stream and per-connection, credit-based, and receiver-driven — the receiver advertises how many bytes it will accept
WINDOW_UPDATE frames grant additional credit; default initial window is 65,535 bytes and applies to DATA frames only (never HEADERS)
Small default window is a classic throughput bug: 64 KB over a 100 ms RTT caps a stream near 5 Mbps regardless of link speed — raise INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE
Flow control lets a client throttle a video stream it has paused without killing the connection or the other streams
CONTINUATION frames carry header blocks too large for one frame; the `CONTINUATION flood` DoS (CVE-2024-27316-class) abused unbounded, uncounted continuation frames
Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487): opening streams and instantly RST_STREAM-ing them let attackers exceed MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS in work terms — mitigated by counting resets and rate-limiting

chapters.title: QUIC: A New Transport on UDP
points: QUIC (RFC 9000) is a general-purpose, connection-oriented, encrypted, multiplexed transport built on top of UDP — HTTP/3 is one application of it
Why UDP and not a new IP protocol: middleboxes (NATs, firewalls, load balancers) drop unknown IP protocols; ossification made TCP unevolvable, so QUIC hides inside UDP datagrams
QUIC lives in userspace (in the browser or server process), so it can be updated with a software release instead of a kernel or OS upgrade
TLS 1.3 is integrated, not layered: the handshake is carried in QUIC CRYPTO frames and there is no separate TLS record layer
Handshake cost: 1-RTT to first byte for a new connection (vs TCP's 1 RTT + TLS 1.3's 1 RTT = 2), and 0-RTT for resumed connections using a stored ticket
0-RTT data is replayable by an attacker, so it must be restricted to idempotent requests (GET without side effects) — never a POST that charges a card
Nearly the entire packet is encrypted and authenticated, including most of the header; only a few bits and the connection ID are visible to the network
Header protection additionally masks the packet number, blocking middleboxes from tracking or rewriting QUIC internals — deliberate anti-ossification
Connection IDs replace the 4-tuple as connection identity, so a connection survives an IP or port change
Connection migration: switching from Wi-Fi to cellular keeps the same QUIC connection and its congestion state — no re-handshake, no dropped video call
Streams are first-class in the transport: each has its own flow control and its own offset space, allowing independent reassembly and killing transport HOL blocking
QUIC stream IDs encode direction and initiator in the low 2 bits — 0x0 client bidi, 0x1 server bidi, 0x2 client uni, 0x3 server uni
Better loss recovery than TCP: packet numbers never repeat on retransmission, removing TCP's retransmission ambiguity and giving exact RTT samples; plus ACK ranges and explicit ACK delay
Congestion control is pluggable in userspace (NewReno by default in RFC 9002, commonly BBR or CUBIC in practice)
Amplification defense: a server must not send more than 3× the bytes received from an unvalidated client address, blocking QUIC reflection attacks
Frames live inside packets and packets inside UDP datagrams; frame types include STREAM, ACK, CRYPTO, MAX_DATA, NEW_CONNECTION_ID, PATH_CHALLENGE, CONNECTION_CLOSE

chapters.title: HTTP/3 and QPACK
points: HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP semantics mapped onto QUIC: same methods, status codes, and headers; different framing and no reliance on TCP
Division of labor: QUIC owns streams, reliability, flow control, and congestion control, so HTTP/3's own framing layer is far thinner than HTTP/2's
One request/response pair uses exactly one QUIC bidirectional stream — HTTP/3 does not implement multiplexing itself, it inherits it
HTTP/3 frames: HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, GOAWAY, MAX_PUSH_ID; there is no RST_STREAM (QUIC's RESET_STREAM does it) and no WINDOW_UPDATE (QUIC flow control does it)
Unidirectional streams carry control data: one control stream per side plus QPACK encoder and decoder streams, identified by a stream type byte
HPACK cannot be reused, because its dynamic table assumes strictly ordered delivery — with QUIC, header blocks can arrive out of order and would decode against the wrong table state
QPACK (RFC 9204) keeps a static table (now 99 entries, tuned with modern headers) and a dynamic table, but splits table *updates* onto separate unidirectional encoder/decoder streams
Required Insert Count: each header block declares the dynamic-table state it needs; if that state has not arrived yet, decoding of that block blocks — a deliberately bounded, per-block HOL risk
SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS caps how many streams may be blocked this way; setting it to 0 makes decoding never block at the price of worse compression
The tunable trade-off to remember: maximum compression (reference the newest table entries) versus maximum independence (reference only safely-arrived entries)
Base and relative indexing make references position-independent, so an encoder can emit blocks without knowing exact decoder progress
Discovery: a client starts over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 and learns about HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400` response header, then races or upgrades on the next connection
HTTPS/SVCB DNS records (`alpn="h3"`) let a client learn HTTP/3 support before the first connection, removing the Alt-Svc bootstrap round trip
Happy Eyeballs-style racing: browsers attempt QUIC and TCP in parallel and use whichever completes, so a UDP-blocking network degrades rather than fails
HTTP/3 is TLS 1.3-only — there is no cleartext HTTP/3, and the port is still 443 but over UDP

chapters.title: When Each Version Helps (and When It Doesn't)
points: First principle: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 optimize *latency and connection efficiency*, not raw throughput — a single large file download barely changes
HTTP/2 helps most: many small resources, high RTT, low packet loss, a typical wired or good Wi-Fi page load
HTTP/2 helps least or hurts: lossy mobile links (transport HOL), and single-large-file transfers where six connections could grab more bandwidth
HTTP/3 helps most: high loss (>1–2%), mobile and changing networks, high-RTT paths where the saved handshake round trip is real time, and repeat visits that can use 0-RTT
HTTP/3 helps least: clean low-latency links where TCP is already fine — measured gains there are often within noise

HTTP/3 can hurt: networks blocking or throttling UDP, corporate proxies that only understand TCP, and CPU-bound clients — userspace QUIC costs noticeably more CPU per byte than kernel TCP with segmentation offload
CPU note: TCP benefits from decades of NIC offload (TSO/LRO, kernel TLS); QUIC's per-packet userspace crypto is improving with GSO and offloads but is still heavier
Server-to-server on a fast, reliable datacenter link: HTTP/2 (or even HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive) is usually fine; gRPC standardized on HTTP/2 for good reason
gRPC's dependence: it needs HTTP/2 framing for streaming RPC and trailers — this is why HTTP/2 matters far beyond browsers
API traffic with large JSON responses and few requests sees little benefit; chatty APIs with many parallel small calls see a lot
Comparison row — handshake to first byte: HTTP/1.1+TLS1.2 ≈ 3 RTT, HTTP/2+TLS1.3 ≈ 2 RTT, HTTP/3 ≈ 1 RTT, HTTP/3 0-RTT ≈ 0
Comparison row — connections per origin: HTTP/1.1 six, HTTP/2 one, HTTP/3 one (with migration)
Comparison row — header compression: HTTP/1.1 none, HTTP/2 HPACK, HTTP/3 QPACK
Comparison row — network change survives: HTTP/1.1 no, HTTP/2 no, HTTP/3 yes via connection ID
Deployment reality: adopting HTTP/3 is usually a CDN or reverse-proxy toggle, not an application rewrite, since the origin can stay on HTTP/1.1
Rule of thumb for the whole handbook: measure with your real RTT and loss profile — protocol wins are workload-shaped, and vendor benchmarks assume conditions you may not have

chapters.title: Debugging, Gotchas, and Recap
points: Common mistake: leaving HTTP/1.1 optimizations in place after enabling h2 — sharding, spriting, giant bundles, and inlining all fight multiplexing
Common mistake: assuming HTTP/2 fixed all head-of-line blocking; it only fixed the application layer
Common mistake: terminating h2 at the CDN but proxying to origin over HTTP/1.1 without keep-alive, so the slow half dominates
Common mistake: sending uppercase header names or a `Connection: keep-alive` header through an h2 client library — protocol error, not a warning
Common mistake: leaving INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE at 64 KB on high-BDP paths and blaming the network for the throughput ceiling
Common mistake: treating 0-RTT as free — it is replayable, so restrict it to safe, idempotent requests
Common mistake: believing HTTP/3 needs a new port; it is 443/UDP, and firewalls that allow only 443/TCP silently force fallback
Debug tool — curl: `curl --http2 -v`, `curl --http3 -v`; `curl -sI` to read `alt-svc` and confirm h3 advertisement
Debug tool — browser DevTools: add the Protocol column in the Network panel (`h2`, `h3`), and use `chrome://net-export` for a full event log
Debug tool — Wireshark: needs `SSLKEYLOGFILE` to decrypt; for QUIC, use `qlog`/`qvis` since even headers are encrypted on the wire
Debug tool — nghttp/h2load and `nghttp -nv` to dump frames; `quiche`, `msquic`, and `ngtcp2` ship similar client tools for HTTP/3
Measure the right metric: Time to First Byte and Largest Contentful Paint under simulated loss and RTT, not just total bytes
Fallback chain to remember: HTTP/3 attempt fails or times out → HTTP/2 over TCP → HTTP/1.1; clients race so users see degradation, not errors
Security recap: HPACK/QPACK never-indexed literals protect secrets; QUIC's address validation limits amplification; Rapid Reset showed cheap-stream-creation is a DoS surface

One-line recap of the arc: HTTP/2 multiplexed streams onto one TCP connection and compressed headers with HPACK; TCP's ordered byte stream still blocked them, so HTTP/3 rebuilt the transport on UDP as QUIC, moved streams into the transport, integrated TLS 1.3, and adapted header compression as QPACK
Final decision rule: use HTTP/2 everywhere as the baseline, add HTTP/3 at the edge for mobile and lossy users, and keep HTTP/1.1 only as a fallback
